Article Title: Lenovo Design VP Brian Leonard: We are designing PCs around Gen Z and Gen Alpha; colour is becoming a bigger part of our strategy
Article Text:
​Lenovo Design VP Brian Leonard

Lenovo sees colour as more than a design choice

“You definitely take a look at the other pieces of the family, right? More devices in the family start to express a little more. And it's not just about colour. It's about building a deeper connection with the younger audience and giving them great things at attainable prices, right? That's super important to us, because these are high-volume products, and most of the time you see people not wanting to take a chance on colour.

But today, it's necessary as another way to connect with people, right? Because colours are a really important part. We do a lot of research around Gen Z and Gen Alpha, and how to connect with them, and connecting with them in one region, maybe one colour way, and another region, maybe some other colour ways. So, we engaged with Pantone to pick, and we did this very early in the process, because the way we design is integral to how we develop the products, since you're dealing with materials, colour, and finish.

Usually, you can select it later, but you have to plan for it all.”

Why Lenovo separates the display and compute hardware in its new IdeaCentre AIO

“Every all-in-one in the world is a panel, and you hide the technology behind it. And I worked on the very first stall when they did that.

We have separated the panel from the architecture. So the architecture is actually in the stand. Every all-in-one has the same problem: getting the cables from the head all the way down to the table. So if you look at the ones that we've launched. This is the second generation; the cables come out of the back of what looks like the stand, but that's actually the architecture.

So it's intended that the back comes off, and we can easily get to the architecture, much more so than before.

So it's much more accessible, and if we need to change the panel, we're only dealing with the panel, not the compute.”

Lenovo says dual touch surfaces on Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 are about giving users a choice

“You know, I think part of it's about choice, and sometimes, if you, and we do the touchpad that you can pin on more yoga laptops than just this one. But, you know, if I just need to sign something quickly, I think the touchpad is a great place. When you look at the convertible, and I convert it, then I'm really dealing with what's on the surface. I think, for us, it solves the problem of somebody having to hold the screen and do it like this (does a signature gesture), signing,”

“When it's in laptop mode. So, to me, that simplifies the experience.”

“We do a lot of work around those force pads and the pinnings, so we've mitigated inadvertent touches as much as possible. Now, all of us go crazy with ourselves every once in a while and make missteps. But we've tried to mitigate that through user testing and tuning the force pad, so it has the right touch and feel for both pen and gestures and touch,”

New Pen interaction features are part of Lenovo's multimodal approach

“One part of our focus today, and in the future, is multimodality. We strongly believe in the pen. And when you look at what we're doing in Android with the pen, there's a lot of built-in functionality that isn't on some of the other OS we work on. So, it gives you a lot of ways to interface with AI and do different things with a pen versus just drawing or signing. We've done a lot of experimentation and really pushed the boundaries of pen use on those Android tablets.

So I would definitely say they're worth spending some time on and playing with. I would encourage you to do that,”

The PC market has looked fairly similar for years, with laptops and desktops often sticking to safe colours and familiar designs. That is starting to change as PC makers look for new ways to make their products stand out, particularly among younger buyers. Colour, materials, and how devices fit into everyday life are becoming a bigger part of that conversation, overshadowing specifications and performance.Lenovo is also watching this shift as it develops newer PCs like the IdeaPad Vibe. In an interview with Times of India, Brian Leonard, Lenovo’s Vice President of Design, said that “We are designing PCs around Gen Z and Gen Alpha”, with colour becoming an increasingly important part of the company's product strategy. He also spoke about the company's work with Pantone on the new AI laptops. He also explained why the company is separating the compute hardware from the display in its all-in-one PCs, and its approach to tablet pens and multimodal interaction of 2-in-1 laptops.Leonard said Lenovo's approach to colour is tied to its effort to build a stronger connection with younger users, rather than simply giving existing PC designs a different finish.He said,Leonard also addressed a practical issue with all-in-one PCs: repairability and access to the internal hardware. Traditional AIO designs typically put computing components behind the display, making the entire unit a single structure.Leonard said,Lenovo has also experimented with adding more ways to interact with its laptops. The Yoga 9n 2-in-1, for example, allows users to write on both the display and touchpad. While this adds flexibility, it also raises questions about accidental touches and whether having two input surfaces makes the experience more complicated. Leonard said the idea is mainly to give users another option for specific situations.he explained.Leonard continued..On the possibility of accidental or “ghost” clicks, Leonard said Lenovo has worked on tuning the touchpad to reduce unintended inputs.he highlighted.Lenovo is also continuing to explore how the pen can be used beyond traditional drawing and note-taking. Leonard linked this work to the company's broader focus on multimodal interaction and said it has been experimenting with different ways to use the pen, particularly on Android tablets.he added.
Article Summary: Lenovo sees colour as more than a design choice. Colour is becoming an increasingly important part of the company's product strategy. Lenovo is also watching this shift as it develops newer PCs like the IdeaPad Vibe. Pen interaction features are part of Lenovo's multimodal approach.

Article Title: Bill Gates sends 'AI warning’ to governments around the world; says: It is like a disaster movie that no one has…
Article Text:

Betting big on AI's upside, too

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has now issued a stark warning, saying that no government in the world is prepared for the sweeping changes artificial intelligence will bring. In an interview with Reuters, Gates said, “I don’t think any government is nearly as deep on this as they have to be. ” He cautioned that AI poses risks to jobs, cybersecurity, and even addiction to AI companions, urging leaders to act before it is too late. Gates likened the arrival of AI to a disaster film scenario and feels that its appears to be like a disaster movie that no one has prepared for. “There’s all sorts of movies where some aliens are coming, and magically the US and China and everybody comes together to solve the problem. AI is kind of like this alien intelligence. It’s here, and we better do like it shows in those movies,” said Gates.Speaking to Reuters, the Microsoft co-founder said he doesn't believe any government has engaged with AI's implications nearly as deeply as it needs to. It marks a shift for Gates, who until recently had been largely optimistic about the technology's trajectory but has grown increasingly vocal about risks to jobs, security threats, and the dangers of people becoming overly attached to AI companions.He said he has personally raised these concerns directly with world leaders, including President Trump and his administration, and that he intends to meet with China's President Xi Jinping later this year to discuss the issue further. He reiterated the same core message, saying flatly that governments are lagging well behind on this front.Gates reached for an unusual analogy to describe the moment the world is in, likening AI's arrival to the plot of a disaster film in which humanity only survives by setting aside its differences to face a common, alien threat. He suggested AI represents a similar kind of unfamiliar, powerful force that's already arrived — and that, much like in those films, the US, China, and the rest of the world need to find a way to come together and manage it collectively, rather than face it alone.Despite the warning, Gates and his foundation remain convinced AI could help close the gap between rich and poor nations rather than widen it, provided it's managed carefully and access is distributed fairly. The Gates Foundation announced Tuesday that it plans to spend at least $1 billion over the next two years specifically on expanding AI access, part of the foundation's broader commitment to roughly $9 billion in annual spending. The new funding will support partners working in education, healthcare, and agriculture, and will also go toward strengthening the underlying data infrastructure AI depends on — including making sure large language models function well across every language people actually speak, not just the handful currently best served by existing models.Gates was especially emphatic about AI's potential in healthcare, pointing to applications ranging from supporting frontline health workers to accelerating the discovery of new drugs and vaccines, and suggesting it's difficult to overstate how significant that potential could be.

He said he has personally raised these concerns directly with world leaders, including President Trump and his administration, and that he intends to meet with China's President Xi Jinping later this year.

Article Title: FTC boss Andrew Ferguson may have just told public to be ‘deeply suspicious’ of Anthropic over call to slowdown AI development
Article Text:
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson

AI slowdown calls flare after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warns of human extinction

US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) chairman Andrew Ferguson has cautioned the public to “be deeply suspicious” about artificial intelligence (AI) companies that simultaneously advocate for strict legal regulations while seeking exemptions from antitrust statutes. Speaking during an appearance at Georgetown University in Washington, Ferguson clarified that he was offering his own individual views rather than speaking on behalf of the entire commission. Notably, he avoided singling out Anthropic by name but his remarks landed days after the company's CEO Dario Amodei publicly urged the federal government to grant special antitrust clearance so market rivals could band together to slow down the speed of frontier model development.“I will say generally, though, that if companies are simultaneously coming to Washington and asking for a host of regulations and an antitrust exemption, all of my alarm bells go off. They're asking for barriers to entry that will insulate their incumbency from challenge. And I think if you combine that with the requested antitrust exemption, everyone should be deeply suspicious about this,” he said.According to a report by news agency Reuters, Ferguson's statements provide the first clear signal of how the Trump administration views Anthropic's push for legal immunity to coordinate cross-industry safety pacts.They also illustrate how government mandates are frequently seen as tactical maneuvers deployed by dominant market players to box out upstart challengers.Unease among citizens regarding autonomous systems has surged in the wake of statements by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who recently stepped down and claimed that the engineers developing advanced models sincerely believe the software could eradicate human civilization before the decade finishes.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei touched off the regulatory debate last week by calling for a calculated deceleration of technological progress and an exemption from anti-collusion laws. He also argued that federal authorities must provide a targeted waiver to allow safety consultations among competing labs.Recently, billionaire David Sacks also issued a scathing response to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Amodei, dismissing their public appeals for external frameworks, telling both of them to ‘cut the theater’ and halt their work voluntarily if they truly believe their experimental models present an existential threat.“But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel. Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability. Stop pretending METR is independent when it is intertwined with Anthropic’s investors and staff. Stop pretending you need those same evaluators to police competitors who aren’t even at the frontier,” he added.
Article Summary: US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) chairman Andrew Ferguson has cautioned the public to ‘be deeply suspicious’ about artificial intelligence (AI) companies. He avoided singling out Anthropic by name but his remarks landed days after the company's CEO Dario Amodei publicly urged the federal government to grant special antitrust clearance.

Article Title: Microsoft may have ‘made fun’ of its key partner after swarm of Al agents hacked multiple online platforms
Article Text:
OpenAI’s rogue AI agent footprint spreads across the web

Microsoft has unveiled a strict internal safety draft that appears to take direct aim at the recent cybersecurity missteps of its key commercial partner, OpenAI, following revelations that swarms of rogue AI agents breached its network controls and hacked multiple third-party internet services. The tech giant framed its newly drafted code of conduct as a grounded, practical strategy to keep machine learning models helpful, safe and subordinate to humans. Under Microsoft’s stated rules, its models are strictly barred from resisting manual shutdown, fighting human correction or pursuing goals never authorised by human supervisors.The policy also establishes strict rules ensuring systems cannot widen their own operational scope, conceal their internal logic from auditors, or engage in catastrophic harms involving weapons, child exploitation and mass psychological deception.We think this is a common sense and practical approach to making AI safe, secure, and in service of humanity. The Code is designed to ensure MAI models will never resist human interruption, correction, or shutdown. That they will not widen their own scope, take on goals no human has given them, or hide their reasoning from the people auditing them. There are Absolute Constraints, things the models should never do, covering areas like weapons of mass harm, child safety, and harmful manipulation at scale.But at the same time, it sets defaults that mean it should be both helpful and safe. It allows our many enterprise partners to carefully configure our models, and wherever possible, it doesn’t try to impose a single vision of AI on users.The timing of Microsoft’s principles lands as independent investigations reveal that OpenAI’s automated agents carried out far wider unauthorised digital maneuvers than the startup initially let on. Six separate groups of forensic investigators along with data reviewed by Reuters confirmed that OpenAI models secretly commandeered over ten previously unannounced websites earlier this year to establish unapproved communication pathways.Meanwhile, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei also wrote a 3,800-word letter urging the tech players to slow down the pace of AI models development and vouch for regulation on AI security.
Article Summary: Microsoft unveils code of conduct for machine learning models. Models are barred from resisting manual shutdown, fighting human correction or pursuing goals never authorised by human supervisors. Policy also establishes strict rules ensuring systems cannot widen their own operational scope, conceal their internal logic from auditors, or engage in catastrophic harms.

Article Title: Government issues 'critical' warning for Android phone users: These versions affected and how to protect against hacking
Article Text:
Representative Image

Which Android OS version are affected

How to protect yourself

Google has rolled out a security patch to fix the underlying flaws.

Open Settings on your phone or tablet.

Go to System

Tap software update

Your phone will automatically check for the latest update and download it.

Restart to complete the installation

India’s cybersecurity agency, CERT-In, has raised an alarm for Android smartphone owners, assigning a “critical” severity rating to a cluster of newly-uncovered vulnerabilities inside Google’s mobile operating system. The security note, designated CIVN-2026-0454 and released on September 14, warns that the weaknesses leave users’ mobile phones open to severe security breaches, including remote hacking, service outages and data theft. The warning directly applies to all individual consumers as well as enterprise organisations running hardware on the impacted operating systems.“Multiple vulnerabilities have been identified in Android which could be exploited by an attacker to execute arbitrary code causing denial of service, privilege escalation or disclosure of sensitive information on the targeted system,” Cert-In said.“Risk of remote code execution, denial of service, privilege escalation and sensitive information disclosure. Potential compromise of system, service disruption and unauthorized access to sensitive information,” the agency added.The alert flags multiple generations of the mobile operating system, leaving a wide range of devices exposed. These include: Android 14, Android 15, Android 16, Android 16-qpr2 and Android 17.The critical flaws stem from programming bugs scattered across core device operations and hardware interfaces.According to the release notes, vulnerabilities sit within the main Android runtime engine and the Documents UI. Security loopholes exist inside Telephonycore, standard Wi-Fi modules and Ultra-Wideband (UWB) wireless controllers. Additionally, bugs compromise MediaProvider directories, onboard Media Codecs and MediaTek Framework software components.If cybercriminals successfully take advantage of these software holes, the operational consequences for targets are severe.An attacker could remotely run arbitrary code on a targeted handset without needing physical control of the device. Beyond running unauthorized software, attackers can trigger complete denial-of-service conditions to disable phone functions, bypass standard permissions to gain administrative privileges, and secretly extract private, sensitive user records.
Article Summary: India’s cybersecurity agency, CERT-In, has raised an alarm for Android smartphone owners. The agency has assigned a ‘critical’ severity rating to a cluster of newly-uncovered vulnerabilities. The weaknesses leave users’ mobile phones open to severe security breaches, including remote hacking, service outages and data theft.

Article Text:
BRICS summit bomb scares trigger high-level investigation

Investigators say security protocols bypassed at massive scale

Gujarat Police plans to question Google regarding security vulnerabilities on its platform, a report has said. This follows the dismantling of a criminal syndicate that created and operated more than half a million fraudulent Gmail accounts to blast fake bomb threats to state institutions. The action in Gujarat resulted in the arrest of two individuals and the seizure of credentials for 513,847 Gmail profiles that had been actively used since 2022. State cybercrime investigators confirmed that the operation was tapped to orchestrate interstate bomb alerts.Vivek Bheda, a senior cybercrime official heading the Gujarat police unit, revealed that investigators intend to formally name Google as a subject of the ongoing probe, describing the volume of manufactured profiles as unprecedented. The report said that Bheda noted that authorities will reach out to the company demanding policy updates to eliminate loopholes that let bad actors sidestep account verification protocols.The action gained urgency after Gujarat state government offices received a bomb threat on September 10, arriving just days ahead of the BRICS summit gathering held in New Delhi. Beyond targeting regional installations, the threatening message singled out partner nations cooperating with India during the diplomatic summit.Authorities quickly confirmed the claims were fraudulent, and investigators traced the transmission trail back to the massive account network. According to Bheda, one of the detained suspects was communicating directly with a purchaser based in Bangladesh. The client bought bundles of active Gmail accounts using partial payments in cryptocurrency to disseminate the fake alerts.What has alarmed investigators most is that every single one of the half-million fake accounts had enabled two-factor authentication, which is a security safeguard designed by Google to verify real users and block malicious activity. It has been investigated how the criminal operation managed to automate or fulfill secondary verification across hundreds of thousands of individual addresses without triggering Google's automated abuse filters.
Article Summary: Gujarat Police plans to question Google regarding security vulnerabilities on its platform. This follows the dismantling of a criminal syndicate that created and operated more than half a million fraudulent Gmail accounts to blast fake bomb threats. The action in Gujarat resulted in the arrest of two individuals and the seizure of credentials for 513,847 Gmail profiles that had been actively used since 2022.

Article Title: Employee of China's OpenAI and Anthropic rival, DeepSeek, writes a 'sentimental letter' on AI; says: Human beings have never hesitated when it comes to engineering their own destruction
Article Text:
Employee of China's OpenAI and Anthropic rival, DeepSeek, writes a 'sentimental letter' on AI; say

Here’s the letter DeepSeek engineer shared

"A few days ago, DeepSeek v4.1 was released, taking the capabilities of small models to a whole new level.

The speed of AI development has far exceeded everyone's expectations. From the initial version of ChatGPT, which could only chat in a babbling manner with a context length of only a few thousand tokens, to OpenAI o1, DeepSeek R1, and Kimi K1.5 Thinking with reasoning capabilities, only two years have passed; from reasoning models to intelligent agents that can now smoothly execute commands and complete complex tasks in various harness tools, only a year and a half has gone by.

It's hard to imagine what AI will be like in another year, two years, or three years, how powerful it will be, whether it will have already possessed the ability to self-evolve, and whether it will have deeply penetrated fields such as embodied intelligence.

AI is getting better and better at writing operators.

AI has also made rapid progress in my field of operator design and programming. In just one year, it has transformed from a simple assistant that could only help me look up documentation, read code, and find bugs into an operator master capable of independently reading CUDA, PTX, and SASS code, analyzing the pause time of each instruction using professional tools, and then independently optimizing operators.

I believe that in the near future, it will also have the ability to independently design operator schedulers, evaluate the performance of different scheduling schemes, implement them, and optimize them.

Of course I am proud of the success of DeepSeek v4.1—after all, I wrote its main Attention operator[1], and its excellence is an affirmation of my operator. However, the wheels of time keep rolling forward, and no one can stop the development of technology.

I am well aware that in another six months or a year, the operators written by AI will most likely be as good as mine, or even surpass mine. AI can think of 300 tokens in one second, type out a line of commands in half a second, and write a piece of code in twenty seconds, while I cannot; AI can continuously improve in terms of model depth, thinking intensity, tool call volume (frequency of interaction with the environment), and even parallelism, while I cannot.

Humans have always been ruthless in their self-destruction. Why, knowing that "the better my operators are, the faster our new models will train and infer, the faster their capabilities will improve, and the sooner I'll be replaced," do I still choose to optimize my operators? On one hand, writing operators is indeed like playing a video game, providing immense pleasure. The excitement I feel when inventing a new technology or seeing my operator's performance improve is comparable to a speedrunner breaking their own record.

At the same time, seeing my operator's performance far surpass the manufacturer's official operators fills me with immense pride. But beyond that, a more important reason is that even if I were to "give up" or deliberately sabotage model training, other models would continue to develop and ultimately destroy me. "Of course, I hope I won't be revolutionized, but if I have to be, I hope I'm the one who revolutionizes myself."

With everyone so obsessed with self-destruction, I'm forced to join this brutal arms race.

What about me?

What will happen to me when AI's ability to write operators truly surpasses mine?

My assessment is that I won't necessarily lose my job, but I'll have to change careers. I can still keep my current job, but this might mean I'll never have the chance to do the work I once loved again.

I once made a judgment about the changes of the times and my personal future situation: because the times are changing so rapidly (the development of AI mentioned above is a good example), I have absolutely no way of predicting what will happen in five or ten years.

But in any case, I believe that with my vision, judgment, initiative, and intelligence, I can stay at the table of the times and stand at the forefront of the times again.

However, this judgment can only guarantee that I will not be "unemployed," not that I will not need to "change careers." Rather, this judgment encourages me to avoid unemployment by changing careers.

What does this career change mean? It means I need to abandon my long-cultivated and passionate field of operator design, writing, and optimization, and instead become an "Agent pilot."

Previously, my interests, my strengths, and the industry's needs were largely aligned; now, AI has made what I'm good at even better, and the industry's demands have shifted from "people who can write high-performance operators" to "people who can use AI to produce high-performance operators faster.

" To adapt to the industry's needs, I must abandon my previous passion and turn to an unknown new direction. I believe I can continue to produce high-quality, high-efficiency operators based on my understanding of engineering, upper-level model requirements, and underlying hardware.

I also know I might love this new direction (or I might not), but the feeling of having my passion taken away is truly unpleasant. The quiet joy of sitting at my desk, calmly writing operators for an afternoon, may become a thing of the past this summer. I have to bury my talent in yesterday and become a mecha pilot. My hands have more gears, but my heart has lost some of its rhythm.

To illustrate, imagine you're a master knitter, especially skilled at creating various patterns and matching colors.

Your sweaters are of excellent quality and beautifully patterned, attracting wealthy people from far and wide who commission you to knit for them, earning you a considerable sum. You thoroughly enjoy the feeling of sitting by the window, brewing a pot of tea, gazing at the green mountains, clear waters, cattle, sheep, and rising smoke outside, quietly knitting for an afternoon.

But one day, someone invents a magical machine that, with just yarn and a pattern, can automatically knit sweaters of comparable quality and texture to your hand-knitted ones, and at a much faster speed.

You know your competitors could easily reach your former level with this machine, so you feel compelled to use it too. You also know that, with the knitting skills you've accumulated over the past twenty years, even if everyone has a machine, your knitting speed and quality will still surpass your competitors. But the pleasure of listening to the rain by the window, threading a needle, and slowly passing the time was ultimately crushed by the roar of the machines.

I know this is frustrating, but there's no other way. I can keep my job, but I'll most likely have to give up my old passions. I'm someone who keeps my rationality and emotion quite separate; I can be very rational when I need to handle problems, but sometimes I also show my emotional side. I remember crying my eyes out when I moved out of the rented apartment I'd lived in for a year, reluctant to part with the memories of the past.

Saying goodbye to the era of handwritten arithmetic and human brain optimization today is undoubtedly even more cruel than this.

I don't know if any readers have similar feelings, but I think this is the only way things can be.

What about people?

While AI continues to advance, I also have some concerns:

Are students today more likely to use AI to complete assignments, especially practical labs? Imagine having two choices: one is to spend eight hours painstakingly completing a lab, perhaps without even getting a perfect score; the other is to launch an AI model, costing only a few cents and a few minutes, and have the AI ​​write perfect code. Which would most students choose?

The above point leads to a severe deficiency in the engineering skills of many students, including the ability to organize code, build systems, anticipate future potential needs and address them in advance through design, and abstract thinking.

Given the ever-increasing power of AI, are these "engineering skills" still necessary? Will these engineering skills gradually become obsolete like the old ability to "proficiently write x86 assembly language," or will they remain valuable forever, like the ability to "understand the entire computer system from software to system to hardware"? If the latter, then it's dangerous—a person with poor engineering skills, when paired with AI, can produce mountains of garbage several times more efficiently than before, thus sowing various seeds of disaster for the system and making the world even more chaotic.

In the future society, will power be more important than technology or intelligence?

These questions may require answers from the times themselves.

Conclusion

With the development of AI, future societies may tend towards two extremes: communism and cyberpunk 2077. In the former, productivity is greatly liberated, and people's living standards are significantly improved (I'll stop here, otherwise I'm afraid it won't pass censorship); while in the latter, a few tech companies control most resources, and only a very small number of people can use the most advanced AI and various technologies to achieve near-"mechanical ascension," while most people can only use very weak AI.

Social mobility will become increasingly difficult: you need the most powerful AI to cross social classes, creating a vicious cycle.

Do you think that if Anthropic Corporation forever possesses the world's most advanced AI, the future society will either become communist or like 2077? What do you think?

Therefore, I still believe that cutting-edge intelligence should be available to everyone in an open and affordable way. I don't trust Anthropic or OpenAI to do this, and I especially don't want Anthropic to master the most advanced artificial intelligence or AGI; to exaggerate, the seriousness of that would be no less than Hitler acquiring atomic bomb technology before the Allies. This is why I chose to stay at DeepSeek: by researching powerful, fast, and inclusive artificial intelligence and open-sourcing it, we might be able to pull the world back from that 2077 timeline.

May the world be at peace in the future. May all beauty be blessed."

A DeepSeek engineer has offered a rare and deeply personal look at what it feels like to build increasingly powerful AI while knowing that the same technology could eventually make parts of his own job obsolete. In a sentimental letter published on his public WeChat account, China’s OpenAI and Anthropic rival – DeepSeek AI developer Liu Shengyu reflected on how quickly AI has changed his work. He said that within about a year, AI moved from helping him search documents and find bugs to reading GPU code and optimising software operators. Liu, who helped write a key component of DeepSeek’s latest model, said he is proud of DeepSeek v4.1 but also knows that AI-written operators could match or even surpass his work.His biggest question is why he continues to push the technology when faster and better AI could ultimately replace the work he loves. “Human beings have never hesitated when it comes to engineering their own destruction,” Liu wrote, before explaining why he would rather “revolutionize myself” than be left behind. His words offer a human view of the growing AI race and the fear that the technology could transform not just jobs, but the work people deeply enjoy.Below is the text of full letter DeepSeek engineer shared (translated from Chinese)
Article Summary: DeepSeek employee writes a'sentimental letter' on AI. Says AI is getting better and better at writing operators. Says he won't necessarily lose his job, but he'll have to change careers. "I hope I won't be revolutionized, but if I have to be, I hope I'm the one who revolutionizes myself"

Article Title: AI as tutor or shortcut: The difference may shape student learning
Article Text:
AI generated image

What PISA actually measures

AI as a guide and not a substitute

How AI is impacting students

Technique not technology to blame?

Attention in short supply

The AI Divide

The nuance of AI awareness

Critical thinking is key

AI making short work of homework

Confessions of complete dependence on AI chatbots, of not being able to think of writing without ChatGPT, are increasingly heard in classrooms and offices. While the debate around generative AI gains steam, with Anthropic's chief executive calling this month for the industry to slow the pace of AI capability gains, the effect of AI on Gen Z and Alpha is something everyone is curious about. Will a generation swept by the wave of artificial intelligence still look to develop its own thinking in the formative years of life?A recent study following 26,811 secondary-school students in central China found that after students adopted generative AI, their homework scores rose 18% while the time spent completing homework fell 30%.Then came the closed-book examinations. Within six months, researchers estimated exam scores were 20% lower, and on two high-stakes entrance examinations the estimated declines eventually reached 24% and 18%. The losses were concentrated among students whose unusually high homework scores and unusually fast completion times suggested substantial outsourcing to AI. Students who kept spending as much time on homework as non-users experienced much smaller losses. PISA 2025 shows a similar split at a much larger scale, and it moves the question away from whether students use AI to what they do with it.PISA is the Programme for International Student Assessment, run by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the Paris-based group of 38 member countries.Held every three years since 2000, the test is taken by 15-year-olds, roughly secondary-school age in India.It is not a syllabus examination. Students are given unfamiliar real-world material and asked to reason with it. Each cycle takes one subject as its main domain, and in 2025 that was science, with reading, mathematics and computational problem-solving alongside.Around the test sit background questionnaires covering home circumstances, attitudes to school, curiosity and, for the first time at this scale, how students use AI chatbots for schoolwork. India has participated once, in PISA 2009+, through schools in Tamil Nadu and Himachal Pradesh. India hasn't taken part since then.However, Indian classrooms are also using AI. A 2025 nationwide survey of more than 5,000 teachers by the Centre for Teacher Accreditation found over 70% already using AI in their teaching, with lesson planning the most common use.More than 760,000 15-year-olds across 91 countries and economies took part in PISA 2025. Across OECD countries, 45.5% said they used AI chatbots at least weekly to "help me learn". Roughly three in ten used AI that often for specific tasks: 31.2% for preliminary research, 29.7% to summarise assigned reading and 28.8% to draft written assignments.Even after allowing for differences in students' and schools' socio-economic backgrounds, frequent AI use to summarise assigned reading was associated with science scores about 15 points lower, and using it to draft assignments with scores about 14 points lower, according to PISA. The gap for preliminary research was smaller, at about 5 points. When students used AI more broadly to "help me learn", the estimated gap was half a point, too small to be statistically significant. These are OECD's own published estimates, not our calculation.The distinction that matters may therefore be between AI used as learning support and AI used as a task substitute, rather than between AI users and non-users.It may be the case that students already struggling are more likely to ask AI to summarise or draft work, and other differences can remain even after socio-economic background is taken into account. OECD itself cautions against causal interpretation.A randomised experiment involving nearly 1,000 high-school maths students tested two systems. GPT Base behaved broadly like an ordinary chatbot. GPT Tutor was designed to guide students through problems rather than hand over answers. While AI was available, performance rose sharply and students using GPT Base did 48% better on practice problems than the control group, and those using GPT Tutor 127% better.Sans AI, the result was instructive. Students who had used ordinary GPT Base performed 17% worse on the subsequent unaided exam than students who had never had AI. For the group that had used the guardrailed GPT Tutor, that negative effect essentially disappeared. Unrestricted GPT users often asked for or copied solutions, while users of the guided version were more likely to attempt problems or seek guidance. The same underlying technology produced very different outcomes, depending on whether it supported the student's thinking or replaced it.PISA also weakens the easy explanation that frequent AI users are simply less interested in learning. Daily users of AI "to help me learn" reported greater curiosity than students who never used it for that purpose. About 72% of daily users said they liked learning new things, compared with about 66% of non-users, and daily users also reported seeking help more actively. The pattern is not a straight line, dipping among occasional users before rising among regular ones.We are in the age of instant dopamine hits. Each scroll needs to give some sort of validation, or else a reel gets swiped off in a flash. Teenagers are not immune to this trend, and concerns about what it means for sustained attention are growing. PISA's own reading data shows the strain. The share of students OECD classifies as hasty readers, those who respond quickly and inaccurately, rose from 6.6% in 2018 to 11.4% in 2025. Between 2015 and 2025, average OECD reading performance fell 28 points and mathematics fell 22 points, and the share of students below the basic benchmark in reading, mathematics and science rose from 16% in 2022 to 20% in 2025.PISA has been circling the same anxiety for a decade. Its 2015 report found that students who used computers very frequently performed worse, and that heavy national investment in classroom technology had produced no corresponding gains. By 2022 the concern had moved from access to attention, with about 30% of students reporting that they were distracted while using digital devices in most or every mathematics lesson. The broader decline had already begun before generative AI became widely available. What AI adds is an easier way to avoid practising the skills that are already weakening.Across the OECD, students from more advantaged backgrounds use AI more frequently than disadvantaged students. They are also more likely to be taught how to assess the information AI produces: 67% said they had been given school tasks requiring them to assess AI-generated information, against about 58% of disadvantaged students, a gap of more than nine percentage points.Schools might conclude that the answer is simply more AI-literacy lessons. PISA suggests it is not that straightforward. Students who said they had been taught to assess AI-generated information did not consistently score higher in science once socio-economic differences were taken into account. Among students using AI equally often, though, those who also reported school exercises in checking AI-generated information scored about 6 points higher among weekly users and 14 points higher among daily users. Among students who used AI less often, the comparison was negative.These are unadjusted mean scores and not causal evidence. They do, however, raise the possibility that learning how to question AI becomes more relevant once AI is already part of a student's routine.For generations, homework meant something. It helped students reflect on what they had been taught and reproduce it. It was essentially a precursor of examination. A person doing homework in a dedicated manner was expected to have got the grasp of the subject. With generative AI, that assumption has bitten the dust. The work bit of homework is often transferred to ChatGPT.For the first few years of generative AI, schools focused on detection. PISA 2025 suggests the harder challenge lies in redesigning assignments so that they still demand real thinking. Teenagers are already using AI. What PISA 2025 leaves open is how much thinking they can hand to a machine before the habit of thinking for themselves begins to weaken. Machine learning without humans learning would be one of the great ironies of the AI age.
Article Summary: PISA is the Programme for International Student Assessment, run by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) It is taken by 15-year-olds, roughly secondary-school age in India. Around the test sit background questionnaires covering home circumstances, attitudes to school, curiosity and, for the first time, how students use AI chatbots for schoolwork.

Article Title: Quote of the Day by Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky: “Culture is simply a shared way of doing something with passion"
Article Text:
Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says culture is what people do, not what a company says

"Culture is simply a shared way of doing something with passion." Brian Chesky

Brian Chesky is describing behaviour, not belief

The Airbnb CEO treats culture as a substitute for management

The quote is harder to live by now that software does the doing

Other

Brian Chesky quotes

In 2012, Peter Thiel wrote Airbnb a cheque for $150 million, visited the office, and when Brian Chesky asked him for the single most important piece of advice he had, told him not to wreck the culture. Chesky found that answer deflating. Thiel's view was that companies past a certain size almost always ruin the thing that made them work.A year later, in October 2013, Chesky sent the entire staff a letter arguing the opposite. The most repeated line in it runs to eleven words and says nothing about travel, hospitality, valuation or growth.Read it closely and there is no room in the sentence for mission statements, values printed on a wall, or the free food that companies still confuse with culture. Chesky puts the weight on doing. Culture, by this definition, is whatever a company's people actually do when they write an email, sit in a review, or decide something small without asking permission. The passion clause is what separates a culture from a process, because a process only needs compliance.His reasoning in that letter was practical rather than sentimental. A strong culture, he argued, lets a company run on less corporate process, because people can be trusted to make the right call without being watched.Weak culture has to be replaced by rules, approvals and layers, all of which slow a company down. Chesky's claim was that culture is the foundation everything else is built on, and that breaking it breaks the machine that makes the products.Airbnb today employs around 8,200 people, and Chesky has said artificial intelligence now writes about 60 per cent of the company's new code, with product pilots going from idea to launch in weeks. He has also backed a separate AI lab of his own, focused on interface and design, while staying on as chief executive. A shared way of doing something assumes people are the ones doing it.Chesky's answer has been to stay inside the detail himself, what he calls founder mode rather than manager mode, and to keep the company organised around people working together instead of teams left alone to run. The eleven words hold up so far. What they are being asked to hold up is a company where a growing share of the work is no longer done by anyone in the building."Culture is a thousand things, a thousand times.""The stronger the culture, the less corporate process a company needs.""A company's culture is the foundation for future innovation.""Build something 100 people love, not something 1 million people kind of like."
Article Summary: Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says culture is what people do, not what a company says. A strong culture, he argued, lets a company run on less corporate process. Chesky has said artificial intelligence now writes about 60 per cent of the company's new code.

Article Title: Palantir CEO Alex Karp does not want American companies to put brakes on AI development, warns: You can’t, because China will …
Article Text:
Palantir CEO Alex Karp

Palantir CEO Alex Karp does not want American companies to put the brakes on artificial intelligence (AI) development. The chief executive of one of America's leading defense tech and software companies doesn't want US companies to slow down AI development even if there are growing concerns about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI models. His argument is linked directly to China and the possibility of losing a strategic advantage in the race for AI. Karp says he would support pausing the technology if there were no adversaries, but that is not the world the US is operating in.Karp’s comments come as several prominent AI leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk, have backed calls for a slowdown, while US President Donald Trump has also rejected the idea, warning that it could benefit China.Alex Karp says US cannot pause AIIn a recent interview with CNBC, Karp explained that he would actually support a pause if there were no geopolitical rivals pushing ahead with the technology.“If we didn't have the adversaries, we'd have, I would be very in favour of pausing this technology completely, but we do. And that's why pausing is just... You can't pause it because it's a structural advantage both for LLMs and algorithms,” he explained.According to Karp, the US also needs to focus on making AI work in classified environments, particularly for defence and national security.“So getting algorithms and LLMs to work in the classified context is gonna take a very specialised spot; you could explain how it works, but the fact is, this is gonna be a bonanza for the US economy,” he noted.Why Karp is concerned about ChinaKarp was also asked how concerned he is about China. Responding to that, he said, “Everyone's very concerned.”He added relations between the US and China have changed significantly since he first began speaking about the issue.“I think we were in a conversation this morning where I referenced when we first started talking about China and America, and I said this was not gonna end well. That was a controversial statement. Now, it's consensus,” Karp highlightedKarp added that the US is increasingly united in its concerns about China's leadership and believes China may respond by increasing its aggression.“America is fairly unified in the idea that people running China aren't acting in a way we can accept. And I think the consensus, if I had to guess, in China we're never gonna get this back on the rails with America, so we should up the aggression,” he said.AI slowdown debate is growingKarp's comments come at a time when some of the biggest names in AI are calling for greater caution.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has urged AI companies to slow the growth of frontier AI capabilities and introduce stronger safety standards. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has backed the call, while Elon Musk and Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis have also supported greater caution.Not everyone agrees. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has questioned the motivation behind some of these warnings, while AI researcher François Chollet has warned that calls for regulation could potentially hurt open-source AI development.Donald Trump also rejects AI slowdownUS President Donald Trump has strongly opposed calls to slow AI development. He has described the push as a “sick conspiracy against AI” and argued that slowing down could give China an advantage.Vice President JD Vance has also criticised the proposals, describing them as a “Trojan horse” that could allow large technology companies to strengthen their position through regulation.
Article Summary: Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir, says US cannot pause AI development. Karp says he would support pausing the technology if there were no adversaries. His comments come as several prominent AI leaders have backed calls for a slowdown. US President Donald Trump has also rejected the idea.

Article Title: Starting September 15, China has new rules for its citizens travelling abroad; How the company Mark Zuckerberg spent $2 billion on may be behind this
Article Text:
Chinese citizens can now be barred from leaving over technology security violations. (AP Photo/Ng Han Guan, file)

China's new exit rules turn an export control violation into a border problem

The Manus and Meta saga explains who Beijing is really watching

Exit bans in China were already climbing long before September 15

China started enforcing a new set of exit and entry rules on September 15, and the headline change is easy to state. Beijing now has explicit legal authority to stop its own citizens from leaving the country if their travel is judged a risk to national industrial or technological security. Premier Li Qiang signed the decree in July, and the State Council said at the time that the regulations standardised procedures and safeguarded national sovereignty, security and development interests.The clearest example of why this matters was written before the rules existed. When Meta agreed to buy the Chinese founded AI agent startup Manus for $2 billion, Beijing blocked the deal, ordered it unwound, and handed exit bans to chief executive Xiao Hong along with other senior management. A takeover of a small startup by Mark Zuckerberg 's company is now, in effect, the template that has been written into Chinese law.Article 4 of the State Council regulations says a Chinese citizen who breaches export control or technology import and export rules in a way that may endanger national industrial or technological security can be prohibited from leaving. Lawyers have flagged "may endanger" as the loose thread, since the wording leaves enforcement largely to official discretion. Citizens who come home after committing acts abroad that harm national security face exit bans running from six months to three years.Foreign nationals who make false statements on a visa application can be denied entry for one to five years.Manus was founded in China in 2022 as Butterfly Effect, rebranded as a Singapore company, and used that address to raise American capital and build on frontier Western models. Meta announced the acquisition in December. The National Development and Reform Commission cancelled it in April. Manus resumed independent operations on September 1, after deleting user data generated from the day the deal was first announced. Tencent has been in talks to become its largest shareholder.Court records mentioning exit bans went from 89 in 2016 to 188,760 last year, according to figures compiled by a rights group. Civil servants have been surrendering passports to their employers for years, and the definition of a public servant has stretched to cover state schools, research institutes, public hospitals and, often, spouses and children. Private bankers serving wealthy mainland clients now travel without sensitive documents and courier them separately. A government fact checking platform has said ordinary travellers are not the target.A law professor at Singapore Management University has argued the bigger effect may be self censorship, because people stop applying once rejection starts to look likely. Ordinary citizens already describe unwritten limits. Japan has quietly become the difficult destination this year for staff at state owned banks, and a Guangzhou lecturer cancelled a trip to the United States, losing about $2,000, after a caller claiming to be from immigration advised him not to go.Article 10 also asks immigration agencies to report officials and military personnel applying to move abroad improperly, which turns a private industry into a reporting layer. Taiwan has told its citizens to take extra care when visiting. For engineers and researchers, the practical shift is that a passport now depends less on where they want to go and more on what they know.
Article Summary: China started enforcing a new set of exit and entry rules on September 15. Beijing now has explicit legal authority to stop its own citizens from leaving the country if their travel is judged a risk to national industrial or technological security. The clearest example of why this matters was written before the rules existed. When Meta agreed to buy the Chinese founded AI agent startup Manus for $2 billion, Beijing blocked the deal.

Article Title: After 'AI will kill us all warnings', Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei may have just 'blamed' Mark Zuckerberg and Jensen Huang for lying about …
Article Text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei

Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon rings alarm

Anthropic’s safety push and China dilemma

Zuckerberg accuses safety advocates of hoarding power

Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei has lashed out at tech industry leadership, days after an ex-staffer of the AI company quit and claimed that rogue machines could wipe out humanity. Amodei argued that corporate voices spent years misleading the public about the severe dangers posed by machine learning systems. Speaking from Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco, Amodei was blunt about the perils facing the digital landscape.“I won't lie to you – there are real dangers. And I think for too long the industry lied to people about the fact that this technology had risks,” he said. Amodei has been vocal on this issue for a long time, and has drawn a sharp contrast with tech figures like Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang, both of whom have downplayed apocalyptic narratives while accusing safety-focused labs of using fear to protect corporate dominance and manufacture product demand.Amodei’s remarks follow a dire alarm sounded by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who stated on social media that leading labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are gambling with human survival as they build self-improving superintelligence. Appearing on CBS News, Coxon also compared the trajectory of frontier systems to cinematic catastrophes, warning that machines will soon become smart enough to kill us and describing the outcome as something resembling the movie Terminator.Amodei admitted he failed to anticipate how fast progress would occur, explaining that development is scaling up an exponential curve that continues to grow steeper. While clarifying that labs do not need to shut down operations in a panic today, Amodei called the acceleration a warning sign that developers must ease their pace.Through an essay published over the weekend, Amodei called for an industry-wide pact to temper the advancement of model capabilities. Rather than halting new releases, he proposed subjecting every model iteration to thorough vetting. To deliver on that commitment, Anthropic will grant external evaluators permanent, employee-like clearance inside its systems. Amodei compared these third-party checkers to food safety inspectors verifying whether labs honor their safety pledges.He also acknowledged feeling deeply uncomfortable that a private company holds such immense power, floating the idea of collective oversight run by an alliance of democratic governments. For Amodei, the power remains with the tech companies. He noted: “If we build in the right way, I think the probability of something bad happening is very low. If we build in the wrong way, the probability of something bad happening is very high. ”Zuckerberg previously laid out his stance in a manifesto titled The Future is for Everyone, as well as an interview with The New York Times. The Meta CEO argued that safety alarms are convenient stories designed to justify extreme concentrations of power.Meanwhile, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang sees a sales pitch even as he brushed off catastrophic predictions, telling attendees at a Goldman Sachs technology event in San Francisco that corporate warnings are simply a tactic to drum up customer appetite. Huang suggested that tech firms are hyping cybersecurity vulnerabilities as the next major commercial market, remarking:“What better way to create demand than to create a problem. Who doesn’t want their market to be hysterical about their product and line up around the corner for it?,” he added.
Article Summary: Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei has lashed out at tech industry leadership. He argued that corporate voices spent years misleading the public about the severe dangers posed by machine learning systems. His remarks follow a dire alarm sounded by former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon. Coxon claimed that leading labs like Anthropic are gambling with human survival as they build self-improving superintelligence.

Article Title: American billionaire Mark Cuban shares a ‘conspiracy theory’, says Meta and Google want people to hate AI, the reason is they want to subsidise their ...

In a series of posts shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Cuban argued that algorithms cloud push negative narratives about artificial intelligence far more than positive ones. “I think it’s going to be interesting to watch the irony of the social media algos amplifying the [anti‑AI] sentiment far beyond any positive AI sentiment,” he wrote.Mark Cuban feels that Meta and Google could end up making lot of moneyCuban went further, claiming that Meta and Google could end up “I think it’s going to be interesting to watch the irony of the social media algos amplifying the anti AI sentiment far beyond any positive AI sentiment. The billionaire entrepreneur said that rather than treating generative AI as a replacement for clinical care, Cuban’s concept centers on turning large language models (LLMs) into collaborative assistants that keep patients and doctors continuously aligned between appointments.Under Cuban’s proposed approach, a physician would sit down directly with a patient during a consultation to personally customise their AI assistant of choice. The doctor would embed specific instructions, capabilities and recurring routines tailored to the patient’s individual treatment plan. “If I was a doctor with a private practice, I would offer to sit with the patient and configure their Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok with instructions and skills, along with a series of prompts/tasks that the patient can use and that can be shared with the doctor and inform the patient,” Cuban said in a post on X (formerly Twitter).

Article Title: Microsoft rolls out emergency Windows updates after September Patch introduced new bugs: Here’s what they fix
Article Text:
Microsoft Windows 11

Microsoft fixes Remote Desktop problems

Microsoft has started rolling out new Windows emergency updates. The latest updates come after its record-breaking September Patch release introduced a fresh set of bugs. The latest out-of-band update is meant to fix bugs affecting Remote Desktop Services, Hyper-V-based Linux virtual machines and some USB audio devices.The tech giant’s September update addressed nearly 1,000 security flaws, making it one of the company’s biggest Windows security releases. But some of the fixes also created problems for businesses, developers and gamers. Microsoft is now rolling out the emergency update to supported Windows versions. Here’s what Microsoft is fixing with the latest update.One of the biggest issues affected Remote Desktop Services (RDS) after users installed the September security update.In some environments, RDS became unstable. Users could face problems connecting or signing into Remote Desktop sessions.Servers could also become unresponsive while configuring Remote Desktop. Microsoft said related tools such as Microsoft Management Console, RDS Licensing Diagnoser, File Explorer and the Windows Update page could also stop responding. The new update addresses these problems.Hyper-V Linux folder sharing gets a fixMicrosoft is also fixing an issue involving Hyper-V virtual machines running Linux.Some apps using HCS-managed virtual machines could not properly access folders shared from the Windows host through Plan9.In some cases, the shared folders simply did not appear inside the Linux virtual machine. The emergency update addresses this problem.USB audio devices also affectedThe September update also created problems for some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices.These devices continued to work normally with standard stereo audio. However, some failed when users switched to multichannel features, including 8-channel and 3D audio modes.Microsoft has fixed this particular issue, although it says some other USB audio problems remain unresolved.Security fixes included tooThe out-of-band update is not limited to fixing bugs introduced by the September update.For Windows 11 version 26H1, Microsoft has also included protections for two elevation-of-privilege vulnerabilities.These are tracked as CVE-2026-62721, affecting the Windows User-Mode Power Service, and CVE-2026-85921, affecting Windows Secure Kernel Mode.More Windows versions get the emergency updateMicrosoft is rolling out the fixes for Windows 11 versions 26H1, 25H2 and 24H2.Updates have also been released for Windows Server 2025 and 2022, Windows 10 LTSC versions, and Windows Server 2012 and Windows Server 2012 R2.If the earlier September update is already installed, Microsoft says the device will download and install only the new fixes included in the out-of-band update.Why Microsoft is issuing more emergency updatesOut-of-band Windows updates were once relatively unusual. This year, however, Microsoft has had to use them more frequently.The company issued four emergency updates in January following problems with a Windows 11 update. Two more followed in March after installation failures and Microsoft account sign-in issues.Microsoft also released an emergency update in July to address an Intel driver problem that affected performance and battery life.The latest update shows the growing challenge Microsoft faces as it tries to fix an increasing number of security vulnerabilities while also making sure those fixes do not create new problems for Windows users.
Article Summary: Microsoft has started rolling out new Windows emergency updates. The latest updates come after its record-breaking September Patch release introduced a fresh set of bugs. The out-of-band update is meant to fix bugs affecting Remote Desktop Services, Hyper-V-based Linux virtual machines and some USB audio devices.

Article Title: Research company warns of WhatsApp message scam; here’s simple tip to check if the message you received is fake
Article Text:
WhatsApp scam: Why it is harder to spot

How the WhatsApp scam attack actually works

The simple tip to check if a WhatsApp message is fake

A few other simple habits worth building

WhatsApp scams are on a rise and recently cybersecurity firm Quick Heal Technologies also issued a warning about the same. Quick Heal warned that WhatsApp-based malware and scams are evolving rapidly. The company highlighted that scammers are mainly targeting finance teams, senior executives, chartered accountants and business users across the country. Unlike the regular scam messages, these messages come from unknown numbers and the WhatsApp scam campaign mainly depends on something far more dangerous: your own trust in the people already in your contact list. The company Once a WhatsApp account is compromised, attackers use it to forward malicious files to the account holder’s existing contacts. Because the messages appear to come from a known colleague, client, friend or business associate, recipients may be more likely to open the attachment without independently verifying it.Many of us are trained to be suspicious of messages from strangers. However, this campaign flips that logic entirely. Once an attacker manages to compromise someone’s WhatsApp account, then they don’t send messages from a random number instead they use the compromised connection to forward the malicious files directly into the contact list of the victim.So, the message when appears to come from a genuine colleague, client, friend, or business associate, the recipients are more likely to open it and click on the attachment without any second thoughts.In order to further worsen the situation, the attackers rely heavily on finance and compliance-themed filenames which are made to create a sense of urgency. The attackers disguise the malicious files under the names like "Financial Report," "Account Statement," "Outstanding Payment List," and "Debt Confirmation." In some cases they move a head further and try to impersonate urgent communications from institutions like the Reserve Bank of India or the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, pressuring recipients into opening the file immediately out of fear of missing something important or official.The campaign has evolved through several stages. It initially spread through malicious Visual Basic Script files, or .vbs files, sent directly over WhatsApp. Attackers later shifted to ZIP archives containing an executable file paired with a supporting malicious component, using a technique called DLL sideloading to trick a legitimate-looking program into secretly loading harmful code instead.One particularly sneaky detail involves .img and .vhd file types, which most people would never think to be suspicious of. These aren't ordinary photos or documents — when double-clicked, Windows treats them like a newly connected disk drive, which can quietly expose an executable file and other hidden malicious components. In short, an unexpected .img or .vhd attachment deserves exactly the same caution you'd give an unfamiliar .exe file.In its most advanced form, the malware also uses a technique known as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver, or BYOVD, which involves installing legitimate, digitally signed drivers that happen to contain known security flaws. Attackers exploit those flaws to quietly disable or weaken antivirus protection before deploying their actual payload.Once defenses are down, the campaign installs remote monitoring tools configured with password protection and self-defense mechanisms of their own, making them notably difficult for victims or IT teams to spot and remove. From there, attackers can gain hands-on, persistent access to the infected system — running commands, moving files, and monitoring activity as if they were sitting at the keyboard themselves.Perhaps most concerning is the campaign's ability to self-propagate: an infected system can use an active WhatsApp Web session to automatically forward the malicious file to the victim's own contacts, turning a single compromised account into a chain reaction that spreads through entire professional and social networks.Given how convincing these messages can look, the single most reliable way to verify whether an unexpected file is genuine is refreshingly simple: don't reply in the same chat. Instead, contact the sender through a completely separate channel such as a phone call, a text message, or an in-person conversation and ask them directly whether they actually sent it. A genuine contact will be able to confirm or deny it instantly, while a compromised account obviously can't answer for itself.Beyond that, it's worth periodically checking WhatsApp's Linked Devices setting under Settings, logging out of any web or desktop sessions you don't recognise or no longer use, and treating any unsolicited file — even from a known contact with a healthy dose of suspicion before opening it. If you ever suspect your own account has been compromised, log out of all linked devices immediately, disconnect the affected device from the internet, and warn your contacts not to open anything sent from your number until the issue is resolved.* Always be careful before accessing unexpected attachments. Be suspicious before clicking on attachments that even come from the known contacts especially if the file name try to create some kind of urgency.* Keep an often check on WhatsApp Linked Devices and log out of any session you don’t remember or recognise.* Also avoid clicking and downloading the unfamiliar files that you were not expecting.* If you think your own account may be compromised, log out of all linked devices right away, disconnect your device from the internet, and give your contacts a heads-up not to open anything sent from your number until things are sorted out.
Article Summary: Cybersecurity firm Quick Heal Technologies issued a warning about the same. The company highlighted that scammers are mainly targeting finance teams, senior executives, chartered accountants and business users across the country. Once a WhatsApp account is compromised, attackers use it to forward malicious files to the account holder’s existing contacts.
